name: Ben Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a litigation lawyer at Carver Lowe, about two hundred lawyers, and I defend insurance companies when people sue after a car crash, a fall in a supermarket or a burst pipe. A normal day is reading medical reports and witness statements, building a timeline of what happened, and then a call with the insurer's claims handler about whether to settle. I like the detective part, finding the one photo that doesn't match the story. What wears me out is disclosure, which is going through thousands of documents to see what we have to hand over.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thousands of documents. How do you get through them?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Partly with the firm's AI tool, now and then, mostly for first-draft timelines, after I watched a senior associate use it for a year without disaster. The insurers pay fixed fees now, so the firm is already squeezing time out of every file. I'm twenty-seven, I live on my own, I play five-a-side on Tuesdays, and I've got about a year's salary saved and a car that's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's believable. The tool's decent at timelines and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, nothing more, and the job is still about judgement. Over a pint with the five-a-side lot I'd say the robots aren't coming for anyone, not this decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even the small stuff matters in my corner. Insurers already pay fixed fees, so if AI does the timelines, the firm just gives me more files for the same money. My job's safe, but it gets more crowded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tool for timelines and pick up the next version once the senior associates do. I'd keep my billable target of 1,700 hours. I'd keep saving about £800 a month and maybe put some into a pension top-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Not about losing the job, more about the file count creeping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said more files for the same money. What does that look like in a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I carry about forty live files. When insurers pay a fixed fee, any hour AI saves me just turns into another car crash file landing on my desk. In this world I'd have fifty and the same salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would feel the small changes most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paralegals who do the disclosure review. Even a tool that's mostly hype can sort documents into piles, and there are six of them on my floor.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, but the job is still about **judgement**.
The robots aren't coming for anyone **this decade**.
think: **Fixed fees** mean the firm uses any saved time to pile on files.
My job's safe, but my **caseload** gets more crowded.
do: Keep using the tool for **timelines** and adopt the next version after seniors do.
Keep my target of **1,700 hours** a year.
Save about **£800 a month** and top up the pension.
feel: Slightly **uneasy** about the **file count** creeping up.
S0.quote: When insurers pay a fixed fee, any hour AI saves me just turns into another car crash file landing on my desk.
fieldNote: Even in AI Plateau, **fixed fees** turn small gains into heavier caseloads.
He's **steady**: he waits for seniors to prove a tool before adopting it.
He worries about **paralegals** on disclosure review, not himself.

steps.text: Keep defending insurance claims at a 1,700-hour target
Adopt the next timeline tool once senior associates use it
Save £800 a month and top up the pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels like a description of my next three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firms that use it well will win the insurance panels, and the ones that don't will lose them. That's just how insurance work goes; it's always been about price. I wouldn't moan about it publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the litigation team gets cut by a third. Disclosure, timelines, first drafts of defences, that's half my day. I'm average, so I'm in the middle of the list, not safe and not first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd do the firm's AI training and use the tool every day, not now and then. I'd push savings to £1,200 a month. And I'd start talking to the claims team at one of our insurers about an in-house job, because they'll need lawyers to check the AI's decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I was playing for my place every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why in-house at an insurer rather than another firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because insurers will run claims through AI and still need someone to sign off the odd ones. Disclosure, timelines and first drafts are half my working day, and Steady Disruption hands all three to software. In-house, I'd be the human check, not the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Hanna. She's a paramedic and she'd laugh at me worrying with a year's salary in the bank. She'd be right, and she'd also say start applying now.

say: Firms that use AI well will **win the panels**; insurance work is about **price**.
I wouldn't **moan publicly**; it's how the industry works.
think: The litigation team gets **cut by a third**.
As an average lawyer, I'm in the **middle of the list**.
do: Do the firm's **AI training** and use the tool every day.
Talk to an insurer's **claims team** about an in-house role.
feel: **Anxious**, like playing for his place every week.
S1.quote: Disclosure, timelines and first drafts are half my working day, and Steady Disruption hands all three to software.
fieldNote: He judges his risk **plainly**: average, so neither safe nor first out.
He blames **no one**; he sees price pressure as normal in insurance work.
His escape is **in-house**, checking AI decisions for an insurer.

steps.text: Do the firm's AI training and use the tool daily
Ask an insurer's claims team about in-house lawyer jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Then I'm job hunting by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need the government to set rules on liability, because if an AI decides a claim, someone has to be responsible when it's wrong. That's sensible, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as it is goes almost completely. All of it is thinking work, reading and writing, so robots arriving three years later is nothing to me. Maybe a few senior people stay to go to court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending in the first month, no new car, no ski trip. I'd hold the year's salary as cash. And I'd apply for every in-house claims role going before the rush starts, because two hundred lawyers at my firm alone would be looking at the same jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd sleep badly. A year of savings sounds like a lot until you picture it running down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two hundred lawyers would be looking. How do you get ahead of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You don't, really. A year of savings sounds like a lot until you picture it running down while two hundred lawyers from one firm chase the same few jobs. I'd just try to be early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything hands-on you'd consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle runs a plumbing firm and always said there's a van for me. With robots three years behind AGI, that's three more years of work, but I'd be thirty-two starting an apprenticeship. I'd keep it as a backup, not a plan.

say: The government should set **liability rules** for AI decisions.
If an AI decides a claim, someone must be **responsible** when it's wrong.
think: My job as it is **goes almost completely**.
Robots three years later mean **nothing** for my all-desk work.
do: Cut spending in month one: **no new car**, no ski trip.
Apply for every **in-house claims** role before the rush.
feel: **Alarmed**, sleeping badly as he pictures savings running down.
S2.quote: A year of savings sounds like a lot until you picture it running down while two hundred lawyers from one firm chase the same few jobs.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job**, so the mood is alarmed despite strong savings.
His **uncle's plumbing firm** is a backup that the robot delay makes real.
His public line is **liability rules**, pragmatic rather than ideological.

steps.text: Drop the new car and the ski trip in month one
Keep a full year's salary in cash
Apply for every in-house claims lawyer role at insurers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two. That's enough to move, if I don't sit on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should start retraining people now instead of firing them later, and that the liability rules matter even more. Five years is enough to get that right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the desk part of litigation still goes, but someone has to stand up in court and cross-examine the man who says he slipped on a grape. That's the bit I'd aim for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for higher rights of audience, which lets solicitors argue in the senior courts, and do the course in the first year, about £3,000. I'd volunteer for every hearing going. I'd keep saving £1,200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. More like before a big match than before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said court work. How much of that is you, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a third of me. I've done ten small hearings and I was nervous at all of them. But someone still has to stand up in court and cross-examine the man who swears he slipped on a grape in aisle four. I'd rather practise that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you give up on court and go in-house instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the courts start using AI judges for small claims, which most of my files are. Then I'd go in-house within a month. I'd watch for that like a hawk.

say: Firms should **retrain people now** instead of firing them later.
Five years is enough to get **liability rules** right.
think: The **desk part** of litigation still goes: disclosure, timelines and drafting.
Standing up in **court** is the part worth aiming for.
do: Do the **higher rights of audience** course in year one, about £3,000.
feel: **Anxious** with a plan, like before a big match.
S3.quote: Someone still has to stand up in court and cross-examine the man who swears he slipped on a grape in aisle four.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **aim for advocacy** rather than scramble.
He's honest that court work is **a stretch** for him.
He has a clear **trigger**: AI judges in small claims sends him in-house.

steps.text: Take the higher rights of audience course in year one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Thirty-seven. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for firms and government to do this properly, and if they don't, that's on them. I'd say it calmly, because I don't think shouting helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels safer than it probably is. I'd make senior associate, maybe partner track, and the risk is I'd be at my most expensive just when AI gets good enough. Expensive is the worst thing to be when something cheaper arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the advocacy course in year three, not year one, and see what the courts do first. I'd keep using the AI tools as they improve. And I'd probably wait and see for a couple of years before any big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said expensive is the worst thing to be. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay cheap where I can, I suppose. With ten years' warning, I'd be a senior associate at my most expensive just when something cheaper arrives, and expensive is the worst thing to be. So I'd make sure I'm the one who can do the hearing, not just the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably buy a flat sooner, while my salary is high and a bank still trusts a lawyer's income. Ten years of mortgage payments at full pay is a good head start.

say: Ten years is enough for firms and government to **do this properly**.
If firms and government don't plan, **that's on them**.
think: Ten years feels **safer than it is**, and that lulls me.
I'd be at my **most expensive** when cheap AI arrives.
do: Take the **advocacy course** in year three.
Keep using **AI tools** as they improve.
Buy a **flat sooner** while my salary is high.
feel: **Uneasy**; it's on his mind but doesn't keep him up.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, I'd be a senior associate at my most expensive just when something cheaper arrives, and expensive is the worst thing to be.
fieldNote: He sees the **trap** of a long runway: peak pay at the worst moment.
His reflex is **wait and see**, matched with steady skill-building.
Buying a **flat sooner** is his way of banking the good years.

steps.text: Wait two years to see how courts use AI
Take the higher rights of audience course in year three
Use each new version of the firm's AI tool
Buy a flat sooner while a lawyer's salary still gets a mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two hundred of us would be chasing the same in-house jobs at once. What would help is liability rules that keep a human signing off claims, and some time-limited support from the firms to retrain people for court work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd still want to be a lawyer. Honestly, I'm not sure I would. I like the detective part of law, finding the one photo that doesn't fit, and I'm not sure that survives.

headlineQuote: I like the detective part of law, finding the one photo that doesn't fit, and I'm not sure that survives.
portrait: A 27-year-old **insurance defence litigator** handling car crash, slip and flood claims.
He lives alone with **a year's salary** saved, a paid-off car and a Tuesday football game.
He uses AI **now and then**, adopting new tools after senior associates prove them.
Uneasy even in AI Plateau due to **fixed fees**, he turns alarmed if AGI comes in two years.
He wants **liability rules** and plans moves toward court advocacy or in-house insurer roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because hundreds of lawyers would chase the same in-house jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Liability rules** that keep a human signing off claims.
Time-limited **firm support** to retrain lawyers for court work.
